section_summary: This section documents Japanese colonial narcotics policy in Taiwan from the late 1920s through 1936, including the licensing and compulsory treatment of opium smokers, the suppression of political opposition to the opium monopoly, and medical studies of addiction. It also covers coca cultivation, cocaine and morphine production, surplus drug stocks, and several alleged smuggling networks connecting Taiwan with China, Japan, Southeast Asia, and the Netherlands East Indies. Department of State correspondence, cross-reference sheets, press translations, statistical enclosures, and League of Nations material show continuing American concern that official controls and monopolies might facilitate illicit traffic.

subfiles.title: Granting of New Opium Licenses in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Department of State; Embassy and Consulate General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Taiwan Government-General’s decision on applications by secret opium smokers for licenses and compulsory treatment.
subfiles.summary: The government classified 25,527 applicants as non-addicts, partial addicts requiring treatment, or confirmed addicts requiring further examination. Police chief Ishii describes licensing as a revocable humanitarian concession and promises expanded hospitals, policing, and customs enforcement to eliminate secret smoking and trafficking.

subfiles.title: Opium Licenses
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Department of State; Embassy and Consulate General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports final provincial figures for new opium licenses and discusses rumors concerning illicit licenses and morphine traffic.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau of Federal Police approved 5,486 licenses, directed 1,347 applicants to treatment, and recorded absences and deaths among those examined. Reed questions the effectiveness of warnings and treatment and relays rumors that earlier licenses remained valid and that morphine bearing Japanese official stamps was entering Hsinchu in large quantities.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 70 on the Sagara Maru
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a related file concerning the alleged Sagara Maru opium-smuggling case.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Reed's Despatch 70 from Taihoku: the case against the Sagara Maru was to be tried in Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Opium Smuggling Case to Be Tried in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Describes allegations that the Japanese steamer Sagara Maru carried a very large Persian Gulf opium shipment intended for China.
subfiles.summary: Press accounts say Japanese intermediaries arranged a 2.5-million-yen opium shipment that evaded a Dutch revenue vessel, changed flags and landed near Canton; as Chinese and Japanese officials were implicated, the defendants and master were moved to Taiwan for trial under Vice Consul Yano's escort.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 71 on the Taiwan Minshuto Party
subfiles.about: Points to a report linking the forced dissolution of the Taiwan Minshuto Party to its opposition to official opium policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 71: Reed concludes the Government-General retaliated against the Taiwan Minshuto Party for its opium stance.

subfiles.title: Disbanding of the Minshuto Party
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Analyzes the police dissolution of the Taiwan Minshuto Party and argues that its opposition to the opium monopoly was an important cause.
subfiles.summary: Police dissolved the party, arrested sixteen leaders, and invoked public-order legislation after it adopted a platform demanding political rights, self-government, social reform, prohibition of opium smoking, and abolition of the monopoly. Reed accepts that radical tendencies existed but regards the suppression as partly retaliatory and criticizes the Government-General’s opium revenues, official advisory system, and resistance to Formosan political participation.

subfiles.title: Taiwan Narcotics Laws and Regulations Checklist
subfiles.about: Lists narcotics statutes and regulations believed to be in force in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Checklist of Taiwan narcotics rules: home-affairs orders, 1924 opium regulations, 1928 and 1929 ordinances, enforcement rules and rules applying opium laws in China; State lacks one item believed in force.

subfiles.title: Laws and Regulations Regarding Control of the Traffic in Narcotic Drugs
subfiles.from: Department of State, signed by W. R. Castle Jr. for the Secretary
subfiles.to: American diplomatic officers and certain American consular officers
subfiles.about: Requests authoritative verification and supplementation of questionnaires on narcotics laws throughout foreign and colonial jurisdictions.
subfiles.summary: The Department seeks exact legal information for the Commissioner of Narcotics and for future international reference under narcotics treaties. Officers are instructed to consult local governments, correct errors, obtain summaries and four copies of missing laws, and report territories for which information cannot be secured.

subfiles.title: Annex: Consular Offices and Territories Assigned for Narcotics Reporting
subfiles.about: Assigns colonial, mandated, and dependent territories to particular consular posts for narcotics-law reporting.
subfiles.summary: The annex pairs consular offices from Gibraltar and Calcutta to Taihoku and Danzig with the territories about which each must obtain information. The Taihoku post is assigned Formosa and the Pescadores Islands.

subfiles.title: Japanese Publicly Sell Opium in Formosa
subfiles.from: Hua Pei Jih Pao; translated by FJC
subfiles.about: Reports a Chinese anti-opium official’s accusation that Japan sold opium to Chinese in Formosa while prohibiting Japanese use.
subfiles.summary: Translated clipping: General Chang Chih-chiang alleges Japanese policy deliberately exposed Chinese residents to opium while protecting Japanese nationals, and calls for public education on its harms.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Persia Despatch No. 1363
subfiles.about: References a report that the Formosan Opium Monopoly refused participation in a trade agreement.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Persia Despatch 1363: Japanese Foreign Office officials said the monopoly wouldn't join a trade agreement since opium is a traffic to be controlled.

subfiles.title: Official Government Statistics on Coca and Cocaine Production in Taiwan
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Transmits official statistics on Taiwanese coca cultivation and cocaine manufacture from 1930 through 1933.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham reports that two companies cultivated coca, while only the Taiwan Shoyaku Company manufactured cocaine locally. Production declined while exports rose, and accumulated stocks allowed 1933 exports of crude cocaine to exceed that year’s production.

subfiles.title: Production of Coca and Cocaine in Taiwan, 1930–1933
subfiles.to: American Consulate at Taihoku and Department of State
subfiles.about: Tabulates acreage, coca-leaf output, cocaine manufacture, and exports for 1930–1933.
subfiles.summary: Table: 794 acres of coca at Chikushimon and Shako, declining leaf and cocaine output 1930-1933, mostly exported to Japan with small cocaine shipments to Korea and Kwantung.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Taiwan Coca and Cocaine Statistics to the Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards Ketcham’s despatch and statistics to the Acting Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: State confidentially sends the Treasury Despatch 93 and its enclosure on Taiwan coca-leaf and cocaine production, 1930-1933.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Shanghai Concerning Formosan Cocaine
subfiles.about: Provides Taiwan production data following the seizure at Shanghai of cocaine believed to have been made in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Shanghai sends Ketcham's report for the Consulate General and Treasury Attaché and says Taihoku will report directly to Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Taihoku on Future Narcotics Reporting
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Taiwan cocaine report and orders continued reporting on coca and cocaine production.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Taihoku: the report was valuable and shared with the Bureau of Narcotics and Shanghai; Chinese Customs seized cocaine believed made in Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Reports on the Hoshi Pharmaceutical Interests
subfiles.about: Forwards two older despatches concerning Hajime Hoshi and the Hoshi pharmaceutical companies.
subfiles.summary: Memo links the Hoshi pharmaceutical interests to Formosa coca plantations and cocaine seized at Shanghai, enclosing a 1925 Taihoku and 1927 Tokyo report for the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: Opium Smuggling in Taiwan—Hoshi Drug Company
subfiles.from: Charles L. De Vault, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Gives a detailed account of Hajime Hoshi’s conviction for attempted unlawful importation and sale of a very large opium shipment.
subfiles.summary: Hoshi, Kenkichi Kimura, and Shinji Sekito were fined and held liable for opium valued at ¥1,265,920 after storing it in bonded warehouses and selling it to Shanghai buyers. De Vault describes alleged cooperation or acquiescence by customs and senior Taiwan officials, the partially secret trial, press censorship, and the authorities’ reluctance to prosecute. He concludes that neither Taiwan nor Japan was making a sincere effort to suppress opium smuggling and unlawful exports.

subfiles.title: Police Seizures of Opium in Taiwan, January–June 1925
subfiles.from: Bureau of Police Affairs, Taiwan Government-General
subfiles.about: Lists the dates, types, quantities, and locations of police opium seizures during the first half of 1925.
subfiles.summary: Table of Taiwan opium seizures, January-June 1925, totaling 47,528 momme (about 392 pounds), nearly all Chinese opium.

subfiles.title: Illicit Drug Traffic
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports inquiries into the Japanese source of cocaine smuggled into the United States and Canada.
subfiles.summary: Neville identifies Sankyo, Hoshi Pharmaceutical, and Dai Nippon Seiyaku as Japan’s principal cocaine manufacturers, while noting Hoshi’s legal and financial troubles. He reports a substantial unlicensed trade and requests seized containers and labels so Japanese police can trace illicit production.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Investigation of Drugs Possibly Coming from Formosa
subfiles.about: References an instruction concerning Ydanoff and possible drug shipments from Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Manchuria narcotics file calling for investigation of whether drugs came from Formosa.

subfiles.title: Stocks of Morphine in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports that the Taiwan Monopoly Bureau was seeking a way to dispose of approximately 2,500 pounds of surplus morphine.
subfiles.summary: A decade of morphine production exceeding sales left a stock Japanese pharmaceutical buyers couldn't absorb; conversion to codeine and sale to the Interior Department failed on competition and price, sale to China was sensitive, so the bureau will cut production and fit the surplus into its annual quota.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Report on Surplus Morphine
subfiles.about: Forwards McConaughy’s report on Taiwan’s surplus morphine stocks to the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: Memo sends two copies of Despatch 113 on surplus morphine in Taiwan for confidential use.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and Reporting Instruction on Taiwan Morphine
subfiles.about: Commends McConaughy’s morphine report and requests continuing narcotics intelligence from Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: State rates the report "Very Good," asks information on eventual disposal of the surplus, and wants future narcotics reports in quintuplicate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Amoy Purchase of Formosan Opium
subfiles.about: References an investigation of a major opium purchase in Amoy from Japanese authorities in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: investigation of Chinese purchasers, the Esra brothers and Paul Yip, and proposed action by the American representative on the Opium Advisory Committee.

subfiles.title: Covering Letter for Treasury Attaché Nicholson’s “The Dokikai”
subfiles.from: John W. Bulkley, Bureau of Narcotics
subfiles.to: H. Charles Spruks, Department of State
subfiles.about: Corrects an earlier mailing error involving a Treasury Attaché’s report titled “The Dokikai.”
subfiles.summary: Bulkley says Nicholson's March 20 report was inadvertently enclosed with material on registered addicts in Jiangsu and asks that this letter serve as the proper cover for it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Persian Opium Stored in Formosa
subfiles.about: References a report that Persian opium long stored in Formosa was entering Fujian in small shipments.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Persian opium stored in Formosa since 1931 for political reasons is now reaching Fujian piecemeal.

subfiles.title: Request to the Treasury Concerning Formosan Opium-Addiction Monographs
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Treasury wants copies of medical monographs listed in a League of Nations document and whether it can pay for them.
subfiles.summary: State sends the Treasury League document O.C. 1660 on opium addiction in Formosa and asks desired quantities and cost position before instructing Taihoku to get the monographs.

subfiles.title: Statistical Study in Regard to Opium Addiction in Formosa
subfiles.from: Director of the League of Nations Opium Traffic Section
subfiles.to: Advisory Committee on Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Sōmei Tō’s second statistical report on opium addiction and lists fourteen related medical studies.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the decline of licensed addicts, compulsory hospital treatment, prosecutions, and reduced monopoly sales since 1897. It compares addicts with non-smokers by weight, height, chest measurement, mortality, fertility, occupation, education, and criminality. Its conclusion is that opium damages physical constitution, lowers fertility, raises death rates, and increases certain forms of criminality.

subfiles.title: Treasury Response on Formosan Opium Monographs
subfiles.about: Requests one copy of each Formosan opium monograph for the United States Public Health Service if available without charge.
subfiles.summary: Treasury says the Public Health Service wants all the listed monographs, but the Surgeon General won't pay for them.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Obtain Opium-Research Monographs
subfiles.about: Directs the consul to seek two free copies of each of fifteen studies concerning opium smokers in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Instruction: one set of opium-research monographs stays with State and one goes to Treasury for Public Health Service use; no funds are available to buy them.

subfiles.title: League of Nations List of Formosan Opium-Research Booklets
subfiles.from: League of Nations Opium Traffic Section
subfiles.about: Reproduces the introduction and list of medical booklets that the consul was asked to obtain.
subfiles.summary: The extract identifies Sōmei Tō’s statistical study and fourteen works on abstinence, blood, oral health, congenital habituation, morphine detection, and sexual function. Named researchers include Jintetsu Oh, Kazuo Kubota, Shizuo Kobayashi, Asho Ro, Asho Rin, and Kiroku Rai.

subfiles.title: Drug Traffic: Heroin Arrests at Makassar
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the arrest of two Formosan Chinese travelers at Makassar for alleged heroin smuggling.
subfiles.summary: The suspects, identified in Chinese pronunciation as Tsa Bin Teng and Eu Ten Fu, traveled with a 79-member business tour aboard the Hozan Maru. Maney lists the ship’s extensive East and Southeast Asian itinerary but says his source, Kichijiro Saito, knew no details of the alleged offense.

subfiles.title: Smuggling of Cocaine from Taiwan
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports a Keelung police investigation into a ring allegedly planning large cocaine shipments to South China.
subfiles.summary: Maney, citing the November 28 Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo, says official details await the police inquiry's completion and promises a fuller report.

subfiles.title: Japanese and Foreigners Arrested by Keelung Police in Cocaine Plot
subfiles.to: American Consulate at Taihoku and Department of State
subfiles.about: Describes an alleged multinational conspiracy to import cocaine into Taiwan and reexport it to South China.
subfiles.summary: Keelung police arrested alleged leader Gan Kei Tan and questioned Japanese, Formosans, Chinese, Koreans and foreigners about a planned 100,000-yen cocaine shipment; someone used Horai Katayama's name to sail to Amoy, and fraud and embezzlement complaints were filed against Gan.

subfiles.title: Monographs Concerning Research Work on Opium Smokers in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the instruction to obtain fifteen opium-research monographs and reports that a request has been sent to the Government-General.
subfiles.summary: Maney has asked the Taiwan Government-General's Director General for two copies of each opium-smoker research publication and will forward them later.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 57 on Makassar Heroin Arrests
subfiles.about: Forwards Maney’s report about two Formosan Chinese arrested at Makassar for alleged heroin smuggling.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury two copies of Taihoku Despatch 57 on heroin arrests at Makassar, Celebes, for confidential information.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 56 on Cocaine Smuggling
subfiles.about: Forwards the Taihoku despatch and press translation concerning cocaine smuggling from Taiwan to South China.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury duplicate copies of Despatch 56, Maney's December 2 report on cocaine smuggling with its translated article.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Heroin and Morphine Seizure at Buitenzorg
subfiles.about: References a confidential League document concerning a heroin and morphine seizure at Buitenzorg, Java.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies document O.C.S./Conf./134 and a seizure dated October 27, 1936. It redirects the enclosure to another narcotics file.
